title: The Road to The Crimson City
subtitle: Chapter 5, The Scam Behind the Curtain
text:
The next day Dorothy and the Founder started early in the day and began to get in some steps on their way to the Crimson City. A few hours in, the road began to be rough, and the walking grew so difficult that the Founder often stumbled. He kept trying to sign up people they passed for the platform, but his attempts were uneven, and even the Founder Sales1 were having trouble earning the kind of hockey stick growth both expected.

Sometimes, indeed, the tech-enabled solution had integrations2 that were broken or missing altogether, leaving holes in the product that caused Toto to bark. As for the Founder, having no product-market fit, he kept clumsily pitching3 everyone on his solution they passed. Their disinterest never hurt him, however, and Dorothy would pick him up and set him upon his feet again4, while he joined her in laughing merrily at his own mishap.

As they made their way from the burbs of Kansas City, the strip malls they passed were not nearly as well maintained as they were back home. There were fewer Moment Clinics and fewer trees; the farther they went, the more dismal and lonesome the country became. 5G coverage became spotty at best.

At noon they sat down by the roadside, and Dorothy opened her basket and got out some gluten-free bread. She offered a piece to the Founder, but he refused.

"I am intermittent fasting," he said, "and it is a lucky thing I am, for as much as I’d love to be gluten-free, I really love bread.”

Dorothy immediately saw this was true, so she only nodded and ate her bread.

"Tell me something about yourself and your patient experience with traditional healthcare?" said the Founder when she had finished her dinner. So she told him about Kansas City, how gray everything was there, and how the psoriasis diagnosis and maybe even OCD had turned her life upside down.

The Founder listened carefully and said, "I cannot understand why you should wish to put up with that customer experience. Prior authorization needs to be disrupted."

"That is because you have no healthcare experience" answered the girl. "No matter how dreary and gray our homes are, we people of flesh and blood would rather get responsible healthcare from a reputable hospital and have good insurance. It feels so safe to have good insurance and be able to go to WashU Health System if you need it. There is no insurance coverage as comprehensive as UHS.”

The Founder sighed.

"Of course, I cannot understand it," he said. "If your bank account were stuffed with cash, like mine, you would probably burn money on disrupting traditional care models, and then traditional healthcare would have no customers at all. It is fortunate for United that you have limited capital."

"Won't you tell me a story of how you built InFlames while we are resting?" asked Dorothy.

The Founder looked at her reproachfully and answered:

"My company is so innovative and new that I really know nothing about healthcare, but I started with First Principles, so it’s easier to be really disruptive. I only raised the InFlames seed round the day before yesterday. So what happened in healthcare before I got funded isn’t relevant. Luckily, when the VCs made my term sheet and specified the shares in the option pool, one of the first things he did was to make sure I had equity available for a cofounder so that I could recruit A-players.”

"Now I'll introduce you to my accelerator,'" said the VC. “So he introduced me to my technical cofounder, and as soon as it was finished, I found myself spinning up our platform solution. We use our proprietary technology to disrupt mental health by AI identification of co-occurring inflammation.”

"I think you need a more refined Go-To-Market,'" said the VC. And when the Seed Round was done, we had a much better line-of-sight on our GTM. Then he made the proper intros to other innovators, so I had a lot of fun telling our brand story.”

"This fellow will disrupt the market fast enough,' said the VC. 'He looks just like a Disrupter.'

The VC promoted me on LinkedIn as lead on our raise and set me up on an HLTH panel. Unfortunately, he and his friends soon after walked away and left me to execute.

"I did not like to be deserted this way. So I tried to get them to make some more introductions to payers. But getting my pilot off the ground was hard, and I was forced to keep grinding. It was a lonely life to lead, for I had no work-life balance. Also, it’s my first company, so I don’t have the same network. Many other early-stage companies wanted to steal my ideas, but as soon as they saw my deck, they knew I was doing something innovative. This pleased me and made me feel that I was quite an important person.”

"I felt sad at this, for it showed I was not such a good Founder after all, but the influencers on LinkedIn messaged me, saying, `If you only had product-market-fit demonstrated, you would be as good a CEO as any of them and a better CEO than some of them. Product-market fit is the only Key Result worth having in this Health Tech, no matter whether one is a Founder or a VC.'

"After the crows had gone, I thought this over and decided to try hard to get some product-market fit. By good luck, you came along and signed up, letting me know I had real traction, and from what you say, I am sure the Specialist will give me market insights necessary to achieve hockey stick growth and really disrupt healthcare as soon as we get to the Crimson City."

"I hope so," said Dorothy earnestly, "since you seem anxious to have them."

"Oh, yes; I am anxious," returned the Founder. "It is such an uncomfortable feeling to know one is a fool."

"Well," said the girl, "let us go." And she handed the basket to the Founder.

There were no fences at all by the roadside now, and the land was rough and didn’t even have appropriately demarcated bike lanes to encourage their safe use. Toward evening they came to a Great Forest, Which was the name of a trendy co-working space with many green walls that were intended to attract founders of all kinds before the pandemic. Still, they were mostly empty, and the espresso machines sat unused.

The complex was right in the middle of the road they were supposed to be traveling, so they either had to go through or make this awkward detour neither of them was into. So they decided to open the door and walk into the Great Forrest.

After an hour or so, the natural light faded away, and they found themselves stumbling along in the darkness. Natural light was a great idea in the daytime, but they underestimated the need for artificial lighting, and thus the night was oppressive.

Dorothy could not see at all, but Toto could, for some dogs see very well in the dark, and the Founder declared he could see as well as by day. So she took hold of his arm and managed to get along reasonably well. He pulled out a headlamp and put it on. When he looked down, the lamp got brighter, and when he looked at it, it became dim, so it was not blinding Dorothy with its light. “My friend is also a Founder, and he came up with this great headlamp after realizing that traditional headlamps blind you when you try to look at your friends. He developed it at Burning Man and spent several years perfecting it. I think it's dope.”

"If you see any couch or any place where we crash," she said, "you must tell me; for it is very uncomfortable walking in the dark."

Soon after, the Founder stopped.

“Ahead, it looks like there's an open but abandoned co-working space; you want just to crash there?”

"Yes, indeed," answered the child. "I am all tired out."

The abandoned co-working office had several Aeron Chairs sitting around.

At this point, they both took one Herman Miller chair and then another Herman Miller chair and placed them facing each other and using one in which to sit in the other in which to prop their feet. They promptly passed the heck out.

3Yeah, my pitch is in here. I know, I know. But this is an awkward pitch footnote:

4Mental health for founders is now the real thing. Check out the Founder Mental Health Pledge.
